title: CIty of Las Cruces' Motion to Dismiss El Paso Electric Company's Application for Revision of Retail Electric Rates [Motion]

documents.name: DOC-000369724-26
documents.text:
BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION

IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF EL PASO                             )
ELECTRIC COMPANY FOR REVISION OF ITS RETAIL                             )   Docket No. 25-00082-UT
ELECTRIC RATES PURSUANT TO ADVICE NOTICE                                )
NO. 317                                                                 )

             THE CITY OF LAS CRUCES’ VERIFIED MOTION TO DISMISS
                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY’S APPLICATION
                   FOR REVISION OF RETAIL ELECTRIC RATES

        COMES NOW the City of Las Cruces (the “City” or “CLC”), by and through the

undersigned attorneys, and moves the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (the

“NMPRC” or “Commission” for an order dismissing El Paso Electric Company’s (“Company” or

“EPE”) Application for Revision of Retail Electric Rates (“Application”), filed on March 27, 2026,

pursuant to 17.1.3.9 NMAC, the Commission’s rule on future test year period filing requirements.

EPE’s Application claims to utilize a historical test period but in reality is based on combining

elements of a historical base period filing with elements of a future test year period rate case filing.

        EPE seeks to add $20,271,566 to its base rates for capacity charges under energy storage

agreements (“ESA”) for battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) for the Carne and Santa Teresa

Projects, which were not in operation during the base period or at the time EPE filed its

Application, as well as for New Mexico’s share of capacity charges for the Buena Vista 1 BESS,

which entered service in 2023. This represents 28.7% of the Company’s requested base rate

increase of $70.6 million. Counterintuitively, the addition of costs for these mostly future

dedicated New Mexico resources has resulted in EPE allocating more, not less, of other generation

plant and energy costs to the New Mexico jurisdiction.

        A proper future test year filing might explain this. EPE’s Application does not. EPE has

not attempted to comply with Rule 17.1.3 NMAC’s rigorous requirements for providing historical

base period data, adjusted base period data, “linkage data,” and future test period data. EPE has

not explained nor justified the “linkage” between its request to include these post-test period BESS
 capacity costs and the far-reaching impact of adding new BESS capacity (and related solar energy

production) upon its cost of serving New Mexico customers.

       EPE has not projected the increased loads that have necessitated increasing amounts of

dedicated resources, which a true future test year period filing would encompass. And EPE has

not identified or quantified the projected increases in Texas retail sales and in Texas dedicated

resources that may counterbalance the inter-jurisdictional allocations to New Mexico.

       EPE has presented certain jurisdictional allocation factors that, it says, have been adjusted

for dedicated resources, but it has not explained or demonstrated how it did that. And EPE has

refused to provide in response to discovery requests the data that would allow the parties and Staff

to assess by themselves how proper adjustments for dedicated resources should and could be made.

The Commission should reject EPE’s incomplete application and allow the Company to reapply.

       As grounds for this motion, the City states:

       1.      EPE initiated this docket by filing a motion for a variance allowing it to present two

annual independent audits rather than obtaining an audit covering its intended Base Period of

October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025. In that motion, the Company implied that it would

be utilizing a Historical Test Year Period. See EPE’s Notice Under Rule 17.9.530.11.A and

Verified Petition for Variance, ¶ 1 (citing 17.9.530.7(S)(1) NMAC); see also id. at ¶¶ 9-12 (Dec.

4, 2025).

       2.      Two months later, EPE moved the Commission for a variance from the requirement

that rate case applications be filed within 150 days of the end of the Base Period. In that motion,

EPE again referred to its upcoming rate application as establishing a Historical Test Year Period

pursuant to 17.9.530.7(S)(1) NMAC, which is the historical test year period filing option given to

utilities, as opposed to the future test year period filing option set out in 17.9.530.7(S)(2) NMAC.



                                                 2
 See EPE’s Unopposed and Verified Motion for Variance Regarding Rate Case Filing Deadline, ¶

7 (Feb. 6, 2026).

       3.      The Commission granted both of EPE’s pre-filing motions. See Order Granting

Variance (Dec. 18, 2025); Order Granting Extension of Time (Feb. 19, 2026).

       4.      The cover letter and the “Application for Revision of Retail Rates” pleading that

preface EPE’s rate case filing package describe EPE’s Application as using a Base Period and a

Historical Test Year Period. See, e.g., Cover Letter, p. 1; Application for Revision of Retail

Electric Rates, ¶ 6. So does the testimony of several EPE witnesses. See Direct Testimony of

George Novela at 6:10; Direct Testimony of Steven A. Sierra at 6:3, 6:9; Direct Testimony of

Adrian Hernandez at 6:2; 6:9-15; 26:11, 13; Direct Testimony of Rene F. Gonzalez at 3:2; 4:17-

20; 5:1-18; 14:20 to 15:15.

       5.      The only potential allusion to a future test year period seems to be in the Direct

Testimony of George Novela. He states that EPE is seeking to include costs associated with the

Santa Teresa, Carne and BV1 [Buena Vista 1] battery energy storage systems “that are or will be

effective in the rate year (2027).” Direct Testimony of George Novela at 9:14-17.

       6.      Schedule M-01 presents both EPE’s proposed Allocation Factors for assigning

costs among the New Mexico rate classes and EPE’s proposed jurisdiction allocation factors for

assigning costs between the New Mexico and “Other” jurisdiction, which is comprised primarily

of Texas retail service. See EPE’s Application at Schedule M-01 (PDF pp. 2845-52). The

Application contains no workpapers for Schedule M-1 or M-01.             See Application, passim.

Although EPE witness Adrian Hernandez is identified as sponsor of Schedule M-01, he testifies

that the “specific calculations for each allocator are prepared under the supervision of EPE witness

Soto.” Direct Testimony of Adrian Hernandez at 32:10-11; see also id. at 41:16-19.



                                                 3
        7.      Of specific relevance to EPE’s treatment of the Buena Vista 1, Carne, and Santa

Teresa BESS, Mr. Hernandez also testifies that “[c]onsistent with prior EPE rate case filings,

adjustments were made to the jurisdictional energy and the production demand allocation factors

to reflect certain dedicated facilities in New Mexico and Texas.” Id. at 29:16-18. He added that

Ms. Soto “addresses those adjustments in more detail in her direct testimony.” Id. at 29:18-19.

       8.      EPE witness Enedina Soto testifies that “[g]eneration from EPE’s resources that are

assigned to serve customers from a specific jurisdiction were directly assigned to the relevant

jurisdiction and removed from the retail customers’ energy and demand usage used in the

jurisdictional allocators. For example, Newman Unit 6 is assigned to Texas, and the Carne Project

is assigned to New Mexico.” Direct Testimony of Enedina Soto at 12:9-13.

       9.      Ms. Soto’s reference to the Carne Project is the only hint that EPE included future

generation resources that were not in operation during the Base Period in developing its

jurisdictional allocation factors. See id. After stating that adjustments for dedicated resources are

appropriate because the costs of the generation resources are directly assigned to the relevant

jurisdiction in the jurisdictional cost of service study, she offers as an example the adjustment

made to Holloman Air Force Base’s energy and demand usage to account for the solar photovoltaic

facility that EPE has built to serve the base’s specific load, not to projected future generation

resources dedicated to New Mexico or to Texas. See id. at 13:5-10.

       10.     On April 15, 2026, EPE filed a Notice of Errata and Filing of Replacement Exhibits.

That filing, unlike EPE’s Application, contained a Workpaper M-1. See EPE’s Notice of Errata

and Filing of Replacement Exhibits, at Workpaper M-1 (PDF pp. 1024-1033). However, that

workpaper lists the intra-jurisdictional cost allocation factors for each New Mexico rate class and

does not address the inter-jurisdictional allocation factors for assigning costs to the New Mexico

and Texas (or more accurately “Other”) jurisdictions. See id. As noted in paragraph 6, above,

                                                 4
 Schedule M-01 presents both inter-jurisdictional allocators and intra-class allocators for the New

Mexico jurisdiction.

        11.     On April 23, 2026, the Commission issued a Pre-Hearing Bench Request to EPE.

Among other things, the Commission directed EPE to provide supplemental testimony on the

following questions:

                What are the specific percentage changes in cost allocation for New Mexico

        retail, Texas retail, and wholesale jurisdictions from the Historical Test Year, and

                what is the detailed breakdown of the load driving these changes in the New

        Mexico retail jurisdiction?

Pre-Hearing Bench Request, ¶ 9(o).            The Commission gave EPE the option of providing

supplemental testimony or directing the Commission to the location in previously submitted

testimony where responsive information may be found. See id. at ¶ A.

        12.     On May 7, 2026, EPE witness Soto filed Supplemental Direct Testimony in

response to Paragraph 9(o) of the Pre-Hearing Bench Request.                   See Supplemental Direct

Testimony of Enedina Soto at 1 (May 7, 2026). She testifies that EPE witness Rene Gonzalez’s

Exhibit RFG-01 sets forth the adjustments from the base period for the historical test period for

energy efficiency, year-end customer annualization, and weather [normalization]. 1 See id. at 3:10-

18. She further states that “[i]n addition, there are also differences in the dedicated resource

adjustments that drive the changes in load between the Historical Test Year Period and the Base

Period. These differences are also shown in Exhibit ES-2S.” See id. at 4:1-3.




1 Mr. Gonzalez’s Exhibit RFG-01 was offered, however, for the purpose of demonstrating EPE’s test period

adjustments to revenues, not to support the Company’s inter-jurisdictional or intra-jurisdictional allocation
factors generally. See Direct Testimony of Rene F. Gonzalez at 2:20 to 3:6 & Ex. RFG-1.
                                                     5
        13.     Ms. Soto’s Supplemental Direct Testimony provides tables showing some of the

inter-jurisdictional allocation factors before and after EPE’s adjustment for dedicated resources.

See id. at 3 Table ES-1S & Ex. ES-1S. Ms. Soto also provides tabulations of the New Mexico

class-by-class changes in billing determinants for energy and demand before and after the

Company’s adjustment for dedicated resources, without stating the changes in each class’s

allocation factors. See id. at Ex. ES-2S.

       14.     Exhibit ES-2S of Ms. Soto’s Supplemental Direct Testimony also includes a

tabulation of EPE’s adjustments to monthly energy and capacity values due to individual New

Mexico-dedicated resources. See id. at Ex. ES-2S, p. 3 of 3. This exhibit indicates that EPE

included the Milagro Project as a New Mexico-dedicated resource in the Base Period; under EPE’s

modified 2025 Renewable Energy Act plan approved by the Commission in Case No. 24-00176-

UT, EPE applied the entire output of that facility to New Mexico renewable portfolio standard

compliance from May 2025 through December 2025. See NMPRC Case No. 26-0000024, EPE’s

2025 Renewable Energy Portfolio Report Pursuant to 17.9.572 NMAC, at 10 (May 1, 2026).

Exhibit ES-2 also indicates that for the Test Period, EPE removed the Milagro Project and added

the Carne Project and the Santa Teresa Project. See Supplemental Direct Testimony of Enedina

Soto at Ex. ES-2 nn.2, 3.

       15.     However, the table on the top of page 3 of Exhibit ES-2S purports to show

adjustments for the contributions of the Carne Project and the Santa Teresa Project toward energy

and demand values for the months of October 2024 through December 2025, although neither

project was in operation at that time. See id. at 3. That table also indicates that the adjustments

for the larger 150-MW Santa Teresa Project were smaller than the adjustments for the smaller 130-

MW Carne Project. See id. EPE must be mixing projections with real data. Additionally, one

may surmise that EPE either is mixing up time periods and using partial yearly production for the

                                                6
 Santa Teresa Project or has downrated its Commission-approved solar production capacity from

150,000 kW to 58,000 kW without explanation. See id.

       16.     Ms. Soto’s Supplemental Direct Testimony does not address in a substantive

manner the second part of Bench Request ¶ 9(o): what is the detailed breakdown of the load driving

these changes in the New Mexico retail jurisdiction?      See Supplemental Direct Testimony of

Enedina Soto at 3-4. She refers to her supplemental exhibits without addressing differences in

load that influence the increase of every identified jurisdictional allocation factor from the Base

Period - Before Dedicated Resources Adjustment to the Historical Test Year Period – Before

Dedicated Resources Adjustment values. See id. at Ex. ES-1.

       17.     Ms. Soto also does not address the differences in load and/or in dedicated

generation resources that caused the E1ENERGY allocation to New Mexico to rise significantly

from the Historical Test Year Period - Before Dedicated Resource Adjustment to the Historical

Test Year Period – After Dedicated Resource Adjustment, notwithstanding the fact that EPE would

be replacing energy production from the 150 MW Milagro Project for a partial year with energy

produced by both the 150 MW Santa Teresa Project and the 130 MW Carne Project. See id. It

seems that the answer must lie in even greater amounts of new generation production dedicated to

the Texas jurisdiction, but Ms. Soto provides no information about the Texas side of the

jurisdictional allocation equations.

       18.     The City has propounded discovery requests to EPE seeking real-time information

about EPE’s peak loads, the solar generation output and battery storage capacity of its actual,

operational New Mexico-dedicated resources, and the energy production of all its renewable

resources, including those shared with or dedicated to the Texas jurisdiction. See CLC’s First Set

of Requests for Production of Documents to EPE, at CLC 1-15 (solar production and battery

storage status of Buena Vista 1; 1-27 (hourly New Mexico peak load); 1-30 (deployment of Buena

                                                7
 Vista 1 BESS); 1-38 (Costing Models that record hourly production of each local generation unit,

Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station as a whole, and renewable energy production as a whole).

See CLC’s First Set of Requests for Production of Documents to EPE, attached hereto as Exhibit

A. EPE objected to most of those requests. See EPE’s Objections and Responses to the City’s

First Set of Discovery Requests, attached hereto as Exhibit B. The only actual document that EPE

produced in response to those specific requests for documents was a report on charging and

discharging of the Buena Vista 1 BESS at five-minute intervals. See Exhibit C, attached hereto,

which contains a sample page of that very long spreadsheet, CLC 01-15_Attachment 01.

Otherwise, EPE provided short narrative responses to requests for production of documents or

provided nothing at all. See EPE’s Responses to the City’s First Set of Requests for Production of

Document, Responses to CLC 1-15, 1-27, 1-30, 1-38, attached hereto as Exhibit D.

       19.     Although since June 8, 2026, the City has engaged in telephone calls and email

messages with EPE’s counsel concerning the Company’s inadequate discovery responses and has

received one formal letter from EPE, the Company has produced no additional documents or

information for these or other discovery requests.

       20.     In its Interrogatory and Request for Production Staff 5-10, NMPRC Utility Division

Staff asked EPE to “[p]lease provide all 530 schedules and workpapers in native format with

formulae intact.” See EPE’s Response to Staff’s Fifth Set of Discovery Requests, Response to

Interrogatory and Request for Production Staff 5-10, attached hereto as Exhibit E. EPE produced

numerous attachments corresponding to rate filing schedules, including Staff 05-10_Attachment

15, Schedule M Workpapers. See id. That attachment is a folder containing two spreadsheets.

WP M-01 is an excel spreadsheet version of pages 8 through 10 of the Workpaper M-1 that EPE

filed as part of its Notice of Errata on April 15, 2026. See WP M-01 (in pdf format from excel),

attached hereto as Exhibit F.

                                                8
        21.     The second excel spreadsheet contained in Staff 05-10_Attachment 15 is titled “WP

M-01 – Additional Support.” . See WP M-01 – Additional Support (in pdf format from excel),

attached hereto as Exhibit F. It is a large workbook that includes unadjusted and adjusted monthly

energy and demand data for each New Mexico rate class that were used to develop EPE’s

allocation factors. See id. It also shows the New Mexico adjustments related to each dedicated

New Mexico renewable energy resource. . . including monthly values during the Base Period of

October 2024 through September 2025 for the Carne Solar & BESS and the Santa Teresa Solar &

BESS, although they did not exist during the Base Period and have no historical production

records. See id.

       22.     Notably, while WP M-01 – Additional Support purports to identify the specific

contributions of the non-existent Carne and Santa Teresa Projects, it does not identify or itemize

the contributions of the resources dedicated to other jurisdictions. Instead, these spreadsheets

include a single line labeled “Total Dedicated Resources to Other Jurisdiction.” See, e.g., id. at

33, 34 of 56. This document does not reveal whether these resources dedicated to the other

jurisdiction are gas-fired generation (i.e., Newman Unit 6), renewable energy, battery storage, or

solar paired with BESS. It does not disclose the nameplate capacity of these resources. It does

not identify the imputed capacity value of each resource or the expected monthly, annual, or peak

hour energy production or capacity. It does not reveal whether these resources dedicated to the

other jurisdiction actually existed during any month of the Base Period. It does not reveal when

these resources are anticipated to begin commercial operation.

       23.     Three months after the filing of EPE’s Application for a huge increase in its base

rates, there is neither potential evidence—testimony, exhibits, schedules—presented by the

Company nor data to be gleaned by the intervenors and Staff from EPE’s discovery responses that

explains either the rationale for EPE’s adjustments based on dedicated resources, or the factual

                                                9
 support for EPE’s proposed cost allocations to the New Mexico jurisdiction, or the time frame

over which EPE assumed that dedicated resources would be added to its generation portfolio.

       24.     In effect, EPE is proposing to use a Future Test Year Period rate analysis without

even telling the Commission and the parties when that future period begins and ends.

       25.     Two Commission rules address the use of a future test year period in setting rates

for electric utilities. In both instances, the analysis begins with historical, book data for a twelve-

month period, the Base Period. See 17.9.530.7(F), (S) NMAC; 17.1.3.12 NMAC.

       26.     Under Rule 17.9.530.7(S)(1) NMAC, a utility may elect to present its rate filing

based on a Historical Test Year Period, meaning that it adjusts the Base Period data for

annualizations and known and measurable changes.              See 17.9.530.7(C), (F), (S) NMAC.

Alternatively, under Rule 17.9.530.7(S)(2) NMAC, a utility may elect to present its rate filing

based on a Future Test Year Period, meaning that it adjusts the Base Period data to reflect known

and measurable changes and projections for the twelve-month period immediately following the

end of the historical Base Period. See 17.9.530.7(C), (F), (S) NMAC. Rule 17.9.530 prescribes

the same rate filing requirements and schedules for a Historical Test Year Period filing and a Future

Test Year Period filing when the selected future test year period immediately follows the Base

Period. See 17.9.530.14 NMAC.

       27.     In 2009, the Legislature amended the Public Utility Act to define “future test

period” as “a twelve-month period beginning no later than the date a proposed rate change is

expected to take effect.” NMSA 1978, § 62-3-3(P) (2009). Recognizing the inconsistency

between its own limited scope for a Future Test Year Period, which roughly paralleled the period

for preparation and litigation of a rate application, and the Legislature’s expansion of the future

test period to encompass projections for the period after the proposed new rates would take effect,



                                                  10
 the Commission adopted a new rule to address only rate applications based on the extended future

test period. See 17.1.3 NMAC (effective Feb. 14, 2013).

       28.     The purpose of Rule 17.1.3 NMAC is to “provide for a complete and

comprehensive rate case filing that, by including full explanations and justifications of changes in

items between the adjusted base period, linkage data, and future test period . . . should minimize

the amount of discovery needed by commission staff . . . and intervenors to analyze a filing.”

17.1.3.6 NMAC.

       29.     Rule 17.1.3 NMAC, like Rule 17.9.530 NMAC, begins with a twelve-month

historical base period. Compare 17.2.3.7(B) NMAC with 17.9.530.7(F) NMAC. It interposes a

new requirement for an adjusted base period reflecting annualizations, normalizations, and

adjustments for known and measurable changes and regulatory requirements that occur within the

base period. See 17.1.3.12 NMAC; see also 17.1.3.7(A) NMAC. The separate future test year

period upon which the utility’s requested revenue requirement is based must be supported by

“linkage data,” which is defined as a “specific and detailed description of all line items for the

period of time between the end of the base period and the beginning of the future test year period

required by this rule to create a verifiable link between the future test year period data and base

period data.” 17.1.3.7(H) NMAC; see also 17.1.3.12(D) NMAC.

       30.     While both rules emphasize identification and tracking of costs as opposed to the

development of jurisdictional cost allocations, Rule 17.1.3.17 NMAC broadly requires that the

“future test year period estimates shall be fully explained and linked to the historic base period and

any linkage data.” Furthermore, “[f]or any material changes between base period and future test

year period, cost drivers shall be separately identified, explained and justified as well as linked to

the historical base period and any linkage data.” 17.1.3.17(A) NMAC.



                                                 11
        31.     Section 17 of Rule 17.1.3 NMAC is titled “FUTURE TEST YEAR PERIOD

ESTIMATES SHALL BE FULLY EXPLAINED.” 17.1.3.17 NMAC. After giving examples of

the sort of explanations and “linkage” that the rule requires, that section states that “Staff and other

parties in rate cases should be able to retrace projections back to their historical source, or the new

basis for the estimate should be fully understandable.” 17.1.3.17(C) NMAC. Moreover, “[a]ll

assumptions, escalation factors, contingency provisions and changes in activity levels shall be

quantified and properly supported.” 17.1.3.17(D) NMAC.

       32.     In this Case No. 25-00082-UT, EPE contends that the Carne and Santa Teresa

BESS capacity costs are “known and measurable” and both projects will be in service when EPE’s

proposed rates take effect. See Direct Testimony of Victor Martinez at 19:20-20:8, 21:13-22:3; cf.

Direct Testimony of George Novela at 9:14-17 (EPE is seeking to include costs for the Santa

Teresa, Carne, and Buena Vista 1 BESS systems that “are or will be effective in the rate year

(2027)”.)

       33.     The Commission has not set any definitive limits for the timing of a “known and

measurable change” in a Historical Test Year Period rate case filing, as EPE generally claims this

one to be.    For example, in Case No. 18-00124-UT, the Commission rejected the hearing

examiner’s recommended denial of recovery of the costs of a salary increase for utility employees

on the grounds that the “known and measurable change” had occurred 16 months after the end of

the test period. See NMPRC Case No. 18-00124-UT, Final Order Adopting Recommended

Decision with Modifications, ¶ 12 (July 17, 2019). In that case, the Commission expressly limited

its holding to a salary increase of $57,736, not other expenses or revenues reaching that far beyond

the end of the test year. See id. Among the reasons it gave were that it was a salary expense. See

id. It has been the Commission’s practice to allow salary increases as known and measurable

changes; indeed, EPE is seeking inclusion of salary increases that occurred before the filing of its

                                                  12
 Application but some four or five months after the end of the base period on September 30, 2025.

Cf. Direct Testimony of Steven A. Sierra at 15:13 to 17:13 (EPE’s request includes 4.0% increases

in salaries and wages that took effect in February and March 2026).

        34.     The Commission’s Final Order in Case No. 18-00124-UT did not reject the hearing

examiner’s discussion of previous orders that did not establish definitive time limitations for

known and measurable changes, including one that concluding that “[t]he longer after the end of

the test period adjustments are allowed to be made the more the resulting revenue requirements

become unrepresentative of the test year. Out of test year adjustments, that increase revenue

requirements, do not take into account of other adjustments that may lower revenue requirements.”

NMPRC Case No. 18-00124-UT, Recommended Decision at 15 (June 14, 2019), quoting NMPRC

Case No. 06-00210-UT, Recommended Decision at 60 (May 23, 2007).

        35.     This underlying principles behind allowing, or disallowing, known and measurable

changes to base period data are to make the test period revenue requirement more representative

of the utility’s costs and revenues when the new rates are in effect and to assure that there are no

related adjustments that would lower the revenue requirement. Therefore, EPE should not be

allowed to add the Carne, Santa Teresa, and Buena Vista 1 BESS capacity charges to its base

period expenses merely because they are contractually established. This annual sum of over $20

million is not as simple as a pre-determined increase in salaries for existing employees. The

deployment of the three energy storage facilities has repercussions throughout EPE’s operations

and, consequently, throughout its cost structure.

        36.     Admittedly, three months after its Application was filed EPE provided some

information about the steps it has taken to reflect changes in the costs to serve New Mexico

customers by submitting in a discovery response the “WP M-01 – Additional Support.” But that

information, and that spreadsheet, is too little, too late.

                                                   13
           37.   By pushing very substantial post-base period cost recovery for New Mexico-

dedicated resources into a historical test period rate filing without explaining—and quantifying—

any offsetting reductions in the requested revenue requirement, EPE has submitted a hybrid of a

historical test year period rate application and a future test year period rate application. The

Commission’s rules do not allow that.

          38.   EPE’s hybrid filing lacks the simplicity of a historical test year period rate

application. The Company has not restricted its adjustments to annualizations and normalizations

to reflect the costs and revenues of a full year of service under normal weather conditions. Cf.

17.9.530.7(E) NMAC (defining “annualization”).

          39.   The Company’s proposal to include the Santa Teresa, Carne, and Buena Vista 1

BESS capacity costs implicates operational changes that have far-reaching implications for EPE’s

system operations, costs, and revenues, none of which EPE has addressed in the Application. And

because EPE is a multi-jurisdictional utility, the operational and cost consequences are

complicated by issues of inter-jurisdictional cost allocations, which EPE likewise does not address

except to state that some adjustments were made to allocation factors because of dedicated

resources, two of which were not in service during the base period.

          40.   EPE’s Application therefore should be viewed as a future test year period rate

filing.

          41.   The Commission has established two sets of procedures for future test year period

rate applications. Nowhere in EPE’s Application does the Company suggest that its proposed Test

Year Period filing is meant to reflect its New Mexico customer count, retail energy sales, demand,

or revenues and costs for the future test year period from October 1, 2025 through September 30,

2026. Therefore, EPE has not undertaken a future test year period filing under Rule 17.9.530

NMAC. See 19.9.530.7(S)(2) NMAC. EPE’s allusions to the three BESS facilities being in

                                                14
 operation for a “rate year” of 2027 and its request to include a full year’s worth of capacity charges

for each BESS unit in base rates vaguely hints that the Company’s approach reflects the statutory

outer limit for a future test period, i.e., a twelve-month period beginning no later than the date the

proposed rate change is expected to take effect. See NMSA 1978, § 62-3-3(P); 17.1.3.8(G)

NMAC.      Therefore, Rule 17.1.3 NMAC applies to EPE’s rate application.

       42.     EPE’s Application is totally lacking in the sort of “linkage data” required by Rule

17.1.3 NMAC, as described above in paragraphs 28 through 30. EPE’s “adjustments” to inter-

jurisdictional allocation factors and intra-jurisdictional allocation factors are mentioned in EPE

witness Soto’s Direct Testimony. See supra, ¶¶ 8-9. EPE’s original Workpaper M-01 merely

listed inter-jurisdictional and intra-jurisdictional allocation factors and dollar amounts. See supra,

¶ 10. Ms. Soto’s Supplemental Direct Testimony lists those allocations factors for the Base Period

and the Historical Test Year Period with and without the Dedicated Resources Adjustment and

listed certain input values for those adjustments, without calculations or explanations. See supra,

¶¶ 11-16. EPE’s recent dissemination of an excel workbook labeled “WP M-01 – Additional

Support” belatedly provides some additional data, including actual or projected contributions by

resources dedicated to the New Mexico jurisdiction. See supra, ¶¶ 20-21.

       43.     However, EPE still has not explained how it made adjustments to its inter-

jurisdictional and intra-jurisdictional allocation factors, why it made those adjustments in such a

manner, what were the sources of the data it used in making those adjustments, and whether the

data and the methodologies were applied consistently. See supra, ¶ 14. EPE has not explained

why Ms. Soto only identified the difference in a handful of allocation factors in her Supplemental

Direct Testimony and exhibits. See supra, ¶ 15. And EPE has not provided its calculations for

the unadjusted and adjusted allocation factors.



                                                  15
        44.     EPE’s Application, even as supplemented by its later errata notice filing of

workpapers, its Commission-ordered supplemental direct testimony and exhibits, and its discovery

responses, fails to provide the base period data, adjusted base period data, linkage data, and future

test year period data that Rule 17.1.3 NMAC requires. See supra, ¶¶ 27-30. EPE’s filings in this

case—not just its initial Application package—accomplish quite the opposite of the Commission’s

objectives to enable Staff and intervenors to retrace projections back to their historical source, to

make estimates fully understandable, and to minimize the amount of discovery needed by Staff

and intervenors to analyze the rate filing. See supra, ¶¶ 27, 30.

       45.     EPE’s last general rate proceeding, Case No. 20-00104-UT, utilized a calendar year

2019 historical test period. See NMPRC Case No. 20-00104-UT, Recommended Decision at 29,

144 (Apr. 6, 2021), adopted in relevant part by Final Order Adopting Recommended Decision with

Modifications (June 23, 2021). At that time, the statutory Renewable Portfolio Standard (“RPS”)

was 15 percent of retail energy sales. See NMSA 1978, § 62-16-4(A)(1), (2). In 2019, EPE’s

renewable energy generation fell short of its RPS target, adjusted pursuant to the terms of the then-

current Renewable Energy Act, by about 12 percent. See EPE’s 2019 Annual Renewable Energy

Portfolio Report, at 1, 11 (May 1, 2020). Presently, EPE’s RPS requirement is 40 percent. See

NMSA 1978, § 62-16-4(A)(3).

       46.     In light of the statutorily mandated RPS having grown to 40 percent since EPE’s

base rates were last set and EPE’s procurement of many dedicated renewable energy resources to

fulfill that obligation, one would expect the New Mexico jurisdiction’s share of EPE’s total

company generation and energy costs to have declined. However, Exhibit ES-1S of Ms. Soto’s

Supplemental Direct Testimony indicates that all the jurisdiction allocation factors that she chose

to present increased the costs allocated to New Mexico from the Base Period to the Historical Test

Period, before the Dedicated Resource Adjustment. See Supplemental Direct Testimony of

                                                 16
 Enedina Soto at Ex. ES-1. Including that adjustment, the most important factors for allocating

EPE’s generation-related costs, D1PROD 4CP-A&E and D2PROD 4CP, increased from the Base

Period to the Historical Test Year Period, even though EPE apparently added the yet-to-be-

completed Carne and Santa Teresa Projects after the Base Period. See id. Nowhere does EPE

acknowledge or explain these counterintuitive results.

       47.      Perhaps an even more disturbing trend may be found in comparing EPE’s proposed

inter-jurisdictional allocation factors in the case with those in its previous general rate proceeding,

Case No. 20-00104-UT. Placing EPE’s Schedules M-01 from both cases side-by-side, one sees

that the key allocation factors, including D1PROD 4CP-A&E, D2PROD 4CP, and D2TRAN 4CP,

have increased by approximately three percentage points since the last general rate case, inclusive

of EPE’s Dedicated Resource Adjustment. See Schedule M-01, attached hereto as Exhibit H;

NMPRC Case No. 20-00104-UT Schedule M-01, attached hereto as Exhibit I.

       48.      As EPE’s New Mexico RPS has risen from 15 percent to 40 percent, satisfied

largely with New-Mexico dedicated resources, the Company’s proposal to allocate greater shares

of its costs to New Mexico in addition to the costs of those dedicated resources simply is

inexplicable.   And the resulting proposed revenue requirement increase of over 50 percent is

unacceptable.

       49.      For the foregoing reasons, the City believes that the Commission should reject

EPE’s Application without prejudice pursuant to Rule 17.1.3.9 NMAC. The Commission should

advise EPE of its responsibilities under Rule 17.1.3 NMAC to provide explanations and linkage

data for a future test year rate filing and should put EPE on notice that if it chooses to proceed with

a future test year period rate application, it must produce a base period, an adjusted base period,

linkage data, and a future test year period that encompasses all projected changes in the future test

year period, not selected changes.

of historical data on customer demand with future data about available resources. Nor can it rest

on potentially inconsistent time periods for the determination (or projection) of loads and

resources.

       51.     Finally, in rejecting EPE’s Application, the Commission should put the Company

on notice that additional rate cases expenses engendered by its own inadequate rate application

will not be considered to be prudently incurred.
